title: Nondeterminism
body:
A machine is **nondeterministic** when its transition function may offer several moves on
the same symbol, and the machine is said to accept if *some* sequence of choices leads to
acceptance. Nothing physical corresponds to this. It is a definition chosen because it makes
machines easier to describe, and the interesting question is always the same one: **does it
buy any actual power?**

Two equivalent readings, both used in [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]]:

- **Guessing**: the machine magically picks a winning branch whenever there is a choice.
- **Searching**: the machine explores every branch in parallel, and one of them succeeding
  is enough.

Guessing is the one to think with; searching is the one you implement, and the gap between
them is where the cost hides.

## The answer is different on every rung

This is the fact the course actually tests, and it is not a general law:

| Machine | Does nondeterminism add power? | What it costs to remove |
|---|---|---|
| [[Finite Automata]] | **No.** [[NFA]] → [[DFA]] by the subset construction | up to $2^n$ states |
| [[Pushdown Automata]] | **Yes.** NPDAs are strictly stronger than DPDAs | cannot be removed at all |
| [[Turing Machine]] | **No.** Search the configuration tree | exponential *time* |

The PDA row is the exception and it is the one worth remembering the witness for: even-length
palindromes $\{ww^R\}$. A nondeterministic PDA guesses the midpoint; a deterministic one has
no way to know it has reached the middle, and the stack it would need to check has already
been consumed. So the context-free languages split in two, and only the deterministic half is
what parser generators can use.

The finite-automaton row is the opposite case, and the reason is that a finite automaton's
entire state is finite, so "the set of states I might be in" is itself something a finite
machine can track. That is the whole subset construction in one sentence. A [[Stack]] cannot
be tracked that way, which is exactly why the PDA row comes out differently.

## Power versus time

The Turing row is the important one, because the answer "no extra power" is doing something
sneaky. A deterministic machine simulates a nondeterministic one by breadth-first searching
its tree of configurations, and a tree of depth $t$ with branching factor $b$ has $b^t$
nodes. Same class of languages, exponentially more steps.

That gap has a name. **NP** is the class of problems a nondeterministic machine decides in
polynomial time, equivalently the class where a *guessed* answer can be *checked* in
polynomial time. **P** is what a deterministic machine decides in polynomial time. Whether
the exponential blowup is avoidable in general is the P vs NP question, which lives in
[[NP-Complete]].

So the honest summary: nondeterminism costs nothing in computability and possibly everything
in complexity.

## Where it shows up outside theory

- **Regex engines.** A regex compiles to an [[NFA]], and the engine either simulates the NFA
  directly (tracking a set of states, linear time) or converts to a [[DFA]] first. See
  [[Simulation]].
- **Grammar restrictions.** LL(1) and LR(1) exist to force a nondeterministic parsing
  procedure to be deterministic, by bounding how far ahead it may look.
- **Verification versus solution.** "Easy to check, hard to find" is the guessing reading of
  NP restated in English, and it is why cryptography is possible at all.
- **The list monad.** The searching reading, made executable. In [[Haskell]] a computation
  returning `[a]` returns *every* result rather than choosing one, `[]` is failure, and `>>=`
  is "for each result so far, try every continuation". That is explore-all-branches with a
  type on it, and it is why [[Recursive Backtracking]] in [[PROGRAMMING PARADIGMS]] needs no
  explicit stack and no undo step. See [[Monad]].

## Core Facts to Know

- Nondeterministic acceptance means **some** computation path accepts, not all.
- Two readings: guess the right branch, or explore all branches at once.
- Nondeterminism adds **no power** to a finite automaton (subset construction), at a cost of
  up to $2^n$ states.
- It **does** add power to a [[Pushdown Automata\|PDA]]; the witness is $\{ww^R\}$.
- It adds **no power** to a [[Turing Machine]], but costs exponential time to simulate.
- Power and time are separate questions; the same equivalence can be free in one and
  expensive in the other.
- **NP** = decidable in polynomial time by a nondeterministic machine = checkable in
  polynomial time. See [[NP-Complete]].
